name: norse-mythology

description.en: 44 cards on Norse mythology as the Eddas tell it: the chief gods and what they rule or are known for (Thor → thunder), family ties the Eddas state (Loki's children Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel), Odin's horse, ravens and spear, Thor's hammer, the worlds of gods, humans and giants, Yggdrasil, Bifröst, Valhalla and Ragnarök. Front: a question; back: the answer, in English and Swedish, with the Swedish names in their established form (Oden, Tor, Mjölner). From the Prose and Poetic Eddas in public-domain translations and Wikidata, checked against Nationalencyklopedin and the Swedish Wikipedia.
description.sv: 44 kort om nordisk mytologi så som Eddorna berättar den: de främsta gudarna och vad de råder över eller är kända för (Tor → åskan), släktband som Eddorna anger (Lokes barn Fenrisulven, Midgårdsormen och Hel), Odens häst, korpar och spjut, Tors hammare, gudarnas, människornas och jättarnas världar, Yggdrasil, Bifrost, Valhall och Ragnarök. Framsida: en fråga; baksida: svaret, på engelska och svenska, med de svenska namnen i sin etablerade form (Oden, Tor, Mjölner). Från Snorres Edda och den poetiska Eddan i upphovsrättsfria översättningar och Wikidata, kontrollerat mot Nationalencyklopedin och svenskspråkiga Wikipedia.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (a script that matched every quotation word for word against the saved source texts, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

1. Texts. The two Eddas were downloaded as plain text from Project Gutenberg (queries 1–2): the Prose Edda in Rasmus B. Anderson's translation (1879, eBook #18947), which covers Gylfaginning in full and the main passages of Skáldskaparmál, and the Poetic Edda in Henry Adams Bellows's translation with his notes (1923, eBook #73533). Both translators died more than 70 years ago (Wikidata, query 3). Anderson numbers the paragraphs of Gylfaginning (§1–§59); the locators use those numbers. Bellows's locators name the poem and the stanza, or the note to a stanza.

2. Selection. The cards cover what the editor's brief asked for, as far as both Eddas attest it: the chief gods and what Gylfaginning says each rules or is known for (§20–§33), the family ties stated in the Eddas, Odin's and Thor's best-known possessions, the beings and worlds of the creation story, Yggdrasil, Bifröst, Valhalla and the main events of Ragnarök (§55–§56, Voluspo 44–56). Each candidate fact was kept only if Anderson's Prose Edda states it and, wherever the poems cover it, Bellows's Poetic Edda agrees; see Selection for what was left out.

3. Wikidata. The items were found by their English Wikipedia titles (API call 4, wbgetentities with sites=enwiki), which returned the English, Swedish and multilingual labels and aliases, the Swedish Wikipedia sitelinks and every statement of the items; the labels of the statements' values were fetched in a second call (API call 5). Two exploratory searches by name (wbsearchentities, query 6) came first. The English names on the cards are the Wikidata English label, or an English alias where the label differs from the form the Eddas' translators and the English Wikipedia use (Baldr rather than the label Baldur; Idun, Vidar, Huginn and Muninn); the Swedish names are the Wikidata Swedish label or alias, except where step 4 says otherwise.

4. Swedish. Every Swedish name was compared with the headword of Nationalencyklopedin's article (query 7: the free opening of each article, saved with its URL), with the title of the Swedish Wikipedia article (query 8: the introductions and revision ids, API) and, for names in the poems, with Erik Brate's Swedish Poetic Edda of 1913 (query 9, Project Runeberg). They agree on Oden, Tor, Balder, Loke, Frej, Freja, Njord, Tyr, Heimdall, Idun, Brage, Frigg, Vidar, Höder, Hel, Fenrisulven, Midgårdsormen, Sleipner, Mjölner, Hugin och Munin, Gungner, Bifrost, Yggdrasil, Valhall, Ragnarök, Asgård, Midgård, Jotunheim, Muspelhem, Nifelhem, Surt, Ymer, Mimer and valkyria. NE has no article on Angerboda or Gleipner (the addresses answered with an error page); for these the Swedish Wikipedia titles and the Wikidata Swedish labels agree, and NE's article on Fenrisulven writes "jättekvinnan Angerboda". Thor's mother has no Swedish Wikidata label of her own (the item's Swedish label is "Fjorgyn"); the Swedish form Jord is from the Swedish Wikipedia article Tor ("son till ”allfadern” Oden och asynjan Jord") and Thor's Swedish Wikidata alias "Jords son". Her other names in the card's note are Anderson's English forms Fjorgyn and Hlodyn (Vocabulary and §56); the Swedish forms Fjorgyn and Lodyn are Brate's (Völuspå 56, "Lodyns" and "Fjorgyns son"; query 12), Fjorgyn also being the Wikidata Swedish label and the Swedish Wikipedia title (which writes the other name Lödyn). The Swedish questions and answers were written by the compiler following NE's and Swedish Wikipedia's usage: asarna in lower case, Snorres Edda for the Prose Edda, Ragnarök with a capital as in NE and Wikidata (Brate writes ragnarök). Names in the notes: Jörmungand from the Swedish Wikipedia article Midgårdsormen ("Jörmungand (Jǫrmungandr"; Wikidata's Swedish aliases have only Jörmundgand and similar forms); Svadilfare from the Wikidata Swedish label of Q1125073 and the Swedish Wikipedia article Svadilfare; Ivaldes söner from Anderson's "the sons of Ivalde" (§44) with the Swedish genitive, as NE also writes it (Wikidata's Q37499380 has the Swedish label Ivaldi). The English form Ivaldi in the same note is Bellows's (Grimnismol 43, "Ivaldi’s sons", and his note to it).

5. Cross-check. Every card was checked against at least two sources: the Prose Edda (Anderson) and, where the poems cover the fact, the Poetic Edda (Bellows), plus Wikidata (names and, where it has them, the statement) and Nationalencyklopedin, or the Swedish Wikipedia where NE has no article or does not cover the fact. The evidence of each card quotes what each source says. The script make_dossier.py (query 10) wrote this dossier from the card data: it checks that every quoted passage occurs word for word in the saved copy of its source (the Gutenberg and Runeberg texts, the NE openings and the Wikipedia extracts; in the NE openings, the spaces that removing the HTML tags left before punctuation and inside brackets are removed before comparing and quoting), prints where each Anderson and Bellows quotation stands (chapter, poem, stanza or note) so that the locators could be compared by hand, and writes the Wikidata evidence of each card from its checks and the saved entities, failing if the saved data do not satisfy a check. The scripts themselves are not published; the rules above are what they do.

6. Cards. Fronts are questions in English and Swedish; backs are a name or a short phrase in our own words, with a short note where it helps (for example the meaning of the ravens' names, or how a death at Ragnarök comes about). The answers about what a god rules follow the Prose Edda's own words, shortened: Njord "rules the course of the wind and checks the fury of the sea" → the wind and the sea (the card's note adds that he also checks the fury of fire, so a learner who knows the whole sentence is not misled); Freyr "rules over rain and sunshine, and over the fruits of the earth". English names follow one convention: the familiar anglicised forms of the English translations and of Wikidata's English labels and aliases, written without the Old Norse letter ð and without acute accents (Njord, Tyr, Idun, Vidar, Jord, Angrboda, Hodr, Mimir, Svadilfari), keeping ö only in the four names English usually writes with it (Mjölnir, Jörmungandr, Bifröst, Ragnarök) and the nominative -r where English keeps it (Freyr, Surtr, Huginn). Where an English and a Swedish name differ only in convention, each language has its own form (Baldr/Balder, Fenrir/Fenrisulven, Jörmungandr/Midgårdsormen). Study direction front to back only: several answers recur (Loki answers three cards, Fenrir and Jörmungandr two each), and many fronts are descriptions that would not make sense as answers.

7. Machine checks. For every card the builder checks against live Wikidata that the English and Swedish names on the card are labels or aliases of the item (except where noted in quality control, such as Hodr) and, where Wikidata has the statement, the fact itself: Thor is a thunder deity (P31 Q842697), Freyja a love deity (P31 Q1670614), Tyr's domain is war, Bragi's poetry, Freyr's weather and Loki's deception (P2925); Thor's mother is Jord, Baldr's parents Odin and Frigg, Njord's children Freyr and Freyja, Angrboda's and Loki's children Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel, Sleipnir's mother Loki (P22, P25, P26, P40); Mjölnir is Thor's and Sleipnir and Gungnir Odin's (P127); Odin is killed by Fenrir, Fenrir by Vidar, Thor and Jörmungandr by each other, Baldr by Hodr, Freyr by Surtr and Ymir by Odin (P157); Bifröst is made of the rainbow (P186). Facts Wikidata does not record (Odin's eye, Tyr's hand, Heimdall and Loki killing each other, Idun's apples, the worlds' descriptions) rest on the Eddas and the cross-check in step 5. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (validate_sources.ts).
selection: 44 cards: 11 on the chief gods and what the Prose Edda says they rule or are known for (Odin, Thor, Baldr, Njord, Freyr, Freyja, Tyr, Bragi, Heimdall, Idun, Loki); 8 on family ties stated in the Eddas (Thor's mother Jord, Baldr's parents Odin and Frigg, Njord as father of Freyr and Freyja, Loki's children with Angrboda — Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel — and Loki as the mother of Sleipnir); 8 on beings and things (Mjölnir, Sleipnir, Huginn and Muninn, Gungnir, Gleipnir, the valkyries, Ymir, Surtr); 9 on the world (Yggdrasil, Bifröst, Valhalla, Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim, Ragnarök); and 8 on stories (Odin's eye, Tyr's hand, the death of Baldr, and who kills whom at Ragnarök). Included only what the Eddas themselves state, with nothing from later retellings, folklore or modern popular culture. Left out: the list of the nine worlds, which neither Edda gives (Bellows's note to Voluspo 2 lists eight and calls the ninth "uncertain"), and with it Vanaheim, Alfheim, Svartalfheim and Nidavellir; minor gods and goddesses about whom the Eddas say little (Ull, Forseti, Vali, Hermod, Sif, Nanna, Sigyn, Skadi and the goddesses of Gylfaginning §36) and Frigg, apart from her place as Baldr's mother; claims on which the sources differ, such as Tyr's father (Odin in Snorri, the giant Hymir in Hymiskvitha), Heimdall's mothers or the fate of Mimir's head; and interpretations that are not in the Eddas (Odin as god of war or of the dead, Freyr and Freyja as fertility gods, Loki as a fire god), although the notes keep the Eddas' own statements, such as Freyja's half of the slain. Thor's link to thunder is given by his name and by both translators (Bellows: "the thunder-god"; Anderson's vocabulary: "The god of thunder"), not spelled out in Snorri's description of him, which calls him the strongest of gods and men; the card keeps the universally used answer "thunder" and gives Snorri's description in the note.

licensing: The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content comes from three sources whose terms allow anything: the Prose Edda in Rasmus B. Anderson's translation (1879) and the Poetic Edda in Henry Adams Bellows's translation with his notes (1923), both public domain in the US (Project Gutenberg: "Public domain in the USA") and, since both translators died more than 70 years ago (1936 and 1939), also in countries with a term of life plus 70 years; and Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0, for the English and Swedish names and the statements. The selection of cards is our own (the gods, beings, places and events named in the editor's brief and attested in both Eddas), not taken from any list, and the questions, answers and notes are our own wording of facts; the quotations from the translations are in the evidence, as is allowed for public-domain texts in any case. Erik Brate's Swedish Poetic Edda (1913; Brate died in 1924) is also in the public domain and was used to verify the Swedish name forms; it also supplied the Swedish form Lodyn in one note. Nationalencyklopedin (all rights reserved; its texts may be quoted only non-commercially) and the Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used for verification only: they confirmed the Swedish names and facts the content sources gave, and no wording or selection was taken from them, apart from two single Swedish name forms that the Swedish Wikipedia supplied or confirmed (Jord, also written so in Anderson's translation, and Jörmungand), which are facts and not protected wording; the short passages quoted from them in the provenance report are evidence for the checks, not part of the cards. The CC0 dedication covers the cards only. The quotations from Nationalencyklopedin and the Swedish Wikipedia in the provenance report are short verbatim quotations with their source named, used as evidence under the right of quotation (upphovsrättslagen 22 §) and, for Wikipedia, under CC BY-SA 4.0 with the article and revision cited; they are not released under CC0.

rounds.lens: Sources, licences and machine checks: every card against Anderson's Prose Edda and, where the poems cover it, Bellows's Poetic Edda; the names and statements against Wikidata; the Swedish names against Nationalencyklopedin, the Swedish Wikipedia and Brate's Swedish Edda; every quotation verified word for word against the saved texts by make_dossier.py.
rounds.scope: All 44 cards, the sources and their licences, and the deck metadata.
rounds.summary: Every card is stated in the Prose Edda, and every card the poems cover agrees with the Poetic Edda; Wikidata agrees with the Eddas wherever it has the statement, and NE or the Swedish Wikipedia confirms every Swedish name. No Wikidata check was skipped because Wikidata disagreed with the Eddas; the findings below are differences in naming, gaps in Wikidata or the reference works, and facts left out because the sources differ.

findings.issue: Snorri's description of Thor (Gylfaginning §21) calls him "the strongest of all gods and men" but does not call him a god of thunder; the thunder rests on his name and on the translators' notes (Bellows: "Thor: the thunder-god"; Anderson's vocabulary: "The god of thunder").
findings.resolution: Kept "thunder", as the brief asked and as Wikidata (P31 thunder deity), Bellows, Anderson and the Swedish Wikipedia ("åskgud") give it; Snorri's own description is the back note and the point is explained in Selection.

findings.issue: Wikidata's item for Thor's mother (Q548730, en label "Jörð") has the Swedish label "Fjorgyn", and Thor's P25 also lists a separate item Fjörgyn (Q108807778, normal rank) beside Jörð (preferred rank). NE has no article on her (the address jord gives the article on soil).
findings.resolution: Swedish back "Jord", the form of the Swedish Wikipedia article Tor ("asynjan Jord") and of Thor's Swedish Wikidata alias "Jords son", which the builder checks; no Swedish label check on Q548730. The English "Jörð" is the item's label, and P25 Q548730 is checked. Bellows's note to Voluspo 56 says that the feminine Fjorgyn "apparently refers to Jorth".

findings.issue: Wikidata's English label of Baldr is "Baldur"; Bellows and the English Wikipedia write "Baldr", Anderson "Balder".
findings.resolution: English "Baldr" (an English alias, checked), Swedish "Balder" (label, NE). The same form is used on every card that names him.

findings.issue: Anderson's Prose Edda says only that a mare ran out to the stallion and that Loki later "bore a foal"; that Loki was the mare is stated by Bellows's note to Hyndluljoth 42 and by NE.
findings.resolution: The back (Loki) rests on both Eddas (Gylfaginning §43; Hyndluljoth 42: "And Sleipnir bore he | to Svathilfari"); the note about the mare follows Bellows's note and NE.

findings.issue: Anderson's translation says Odin gave Hel "power over nine worlds", with a footnote that this may be a mistake for "the ninth world".
findings.resolution: The card says only that she rules over the dead in Niflheim, as both readings and Bellows's note agree.

findings.issue: The brief suggested the nine worlds; neither Edda lists them, and Bellows's note to Voluspo 2 lists eight and calls the ninth uncertain.
findings.resolution: No card on the nine worlds or their number; cards only on the five worlds both Eddas describe by name and nature (Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim).

findings.issue: Wikidata's Baldr (Q131658) gives P157 "killed by" Höðr (normal rank) and Loki (deprecated); Frigg's P40 lists Höðr as a deprecated child.
findings.resolution: The card asks who killed Baldr (Höðr, guided by Loki), as both Eddas tell it; the check is on the normal-rank Höðr. The deprecated statements are not used.

findings.issue: Wikidata gives Tyr two fathers, Odin (normal rank) and the giant Hymir (preferred); Snorri makes him Odin's son, Hymiskvitha Hymir's.
findings.resolution: No card on Tyr's father.

findings.issue: Wikidata's domains of Freyr (P2925) are weather and wealth; the Prose Edda says rain, sunshine and the fruits of the earth.
findings.resolution: The back follows the Prose Edda; the builder checks P2925 weather (Q11663), which covers rain and sunshine.

findings.issue: Wikidata's English label is the singular "valkyrie"; the card's answer is the plural.
findings.resolution: Checked the English label "valkyrie" and the Swedish alias "valkyrior" (the Swedish label is "valkyria").

findings.issue: NE has no article Gleipner and none Angerboda (the addresses answered with an error page).
findings.resolution: The Swedish Wikipedia articles Gleipner and Angerboda and the Wikidata Swedish labels confirm the Swedish forms; for Angerboda NE's article Fenrisulven also writes "jättekvinnan Angerboda".

findings.issue: Brate writes ragnarök in lower case; NE, Wikidata and the Swedish Wikipedia article title capitalise it.
findings.resolution: "Ragnarök" with a capital in Swedish throughout, as in NE.

rounds.scope: All 44 cards against Brodeur's independent translation of the Prose Edda, live Wikidata and the Swedish Wikipedia; counts and description.
rounds.summary: No errors found. One ambiguous front (freyja-domain) was tied to the Prose Edda's own words; the description now names the Swedish Wikipedia beside NE; the mistletoe checks are explained in the evidence.

findings.issue: "What is Freyja the goddess of?" has more than one defensible answer: Gylfaginning gives her half of the slain beside love, and NE lists several spheres; only "love" was accepted.
findings.resolution: Verified in Anderson §24 ("it is good to call on her in love affairs"). The front now asks, according to the Prose Edda, in what matters it is good to call on Freyja (sv "I vilka angelägenheter är det enligt Snorres Edda gott att åkalla Freja?"); back "love" / "kärlek"; the note on the slain is kept.

findings.issue: The description says the deck was checked against Nationalencyklopedin, but four cards (thor-mother, hel, gleipnir, ragnarok-heimdall) were checked against the Swedish Wikipedia instead.
findings.resolution: The description now ends "checked against Nationalencyklopedin and the Swedish Wikipedia" / "kontrollerat mot Nationalencyklopedin och svenskspråkiga Wikipedia".

findings.issue: The Wikidata checks on the plant item Viscum album (Q144940) confirm only its common names, and pass only through the capitalised alias "Mistletoe".
findings.resolution: Confirmed live (en alias "Mistletoe", sv label "mistel"). Kept the checks, since the answer is the plant's name, and added to the card's evidence that they only confirm the plant's common names while the story rests on the Eddas and NE.

rounds.reviewer: Claude (AI) — independent Language, translation and language tags reviewer
rounds.scope: All 44 cards, title, description and keywords: English and Swedish wording, name forms against Wikidata, NE, the Swedish Wikipedia and Brate, and language tags.
rounds.summary: Language tags and Swedish names were correct. The English names now follow one stated convention, the calqued Swedish front of ragnarok-thor and four awkward fronts were reworded, Sleipnir is åttabent as in NE, Jord has its own Swedish Wikipedia evidence and the English notes use typographic quotes.

findings.issue: English names mixed anglicised forms (Njord, Tyr, Idun, Vidar) with normalised Old Norse (Jörð, Angrboða, Höðr, Svaðilfari, Mímir, Surtr).
findings.resolution: Adopted the anglicised style the deck mostly used: no ð and no acute accents, ö kept only in Mjölnir, Jörmungandr, Bifröst and Ragnarök, and the nominative -r kept where English keeps it (Freyr, Surtr). Changed Jörð → Jord (thor-mother; Wikidata alias "Jord", checked), Angrboða → Angrboda (angrboda; alias, checked), Höðr → Hodr (baldr-killer; not a Wikidata alias, so the English label check was dropped and the English Wikipedia redirect Hodr → Höðr noted in the evidence), Mímir → Mimir (odin-eye; alias, checked) and Svaðilfari → Svadilfari (sleipnir-mother note). Surtr kept, like Freyr. The convention is stated in the Cards step of the method, and the selection and machine-checks step use the new forms.

findings.issue: The Swedish front calqued "only to" as "bara för att", which in Swedish means "just because" or "just in order to".
findings.resolution: sv "Vilket odjur dödar Tor vid Ragnarök, innan han själv dör av dess gift?"; en "Which monster does Thor kill at Ragnarök before dying of its venom himself?".

findings.issue: "guided by Loki" / "ledd av Loke" could be read as describing Baldr.
findings.resolution: en "Which god, guided by Loki, killed Baldr?"; sv "Vilken gud dödade Balder på Lokes anstiftan?".

findings.issue: The Swedish front repeated "ljus" in two senses.
findings.resolution: sv "Vilken gud är så fager och strålande att det lyser om honom, den bäste av asarna?".

findings.issue: Awkward plural agreement in the English front.
findings.resolution: en "What is the name for the gods' last battle and the destruction of the world?".

findings.issue: "åttafotade" on sleipnir and sleipnir-mother, where NE says "åttabent" / "en häst med åtta ben".
findings.resolution: Both Swedish fronts now say "Odens åttabenta häst".

findings.issue: The Swedish "Jord" was supported in Wikidata only through Thor's alias "Jords son"; the Swedish Wikipedia article on her names Jord directly.
findings.resolution: Fetched today: "Jord (mytologi)" redirects to Fjorgyn (revision 56685825), whose introduction begins "Fjorgyn eller Jord" and says "Hon är känd som moder till Tor"; added as evidence.

findings.issue: English notes used straight quotes (thor-mother, huginn-muninn) while the Swedish notes use typographic ones.
findings.resolution: The English notes now use “earth”, “thought” and “memory”.

rounds.reviewer: Claude (AI) — independent Licensing, attribution and documentation reviewer
rounds.scope: Every source's licence page, every quotation against re-downloaded sources, the method, queries, licensing text and the generated report.
rounds.summary: Licensing was sound. The gungnir evidence now quotes the Anderson sentences that name Ivaldi's sons, the provenance of the Swedish note names is documented, the paragraph range is corrected, the NE wording is gone from the Hugin and Munin note, the licensing text says the report's quotations are not CC0, the quotation check is named in the first method paragraph and the helper scripts' URL templates are recorded. The double numbering of the rendered method was left as in the other decks.

findings.issue: The backNote's "sons of Ivaldi" was supported in the evidence only by NE, a verification source; the Anderson quotation started after the words naming them.
findings.resolution: Verified in pg18947.txt: the Anderson evidence now quotes the full sentence ("Then went Loke to the dwarfs that are called Ivald’s sons, … called Gungner.") and §44 ("Some dwarfs, the sons of Ivalde, made Skidbladner and gave it to Frey."), the source of the Swedish form Ivalde.

findings.issue: The method did not give the provenance of the Swedish note names Jörmungand, Svadilfare and Ivaldes söner, and step 3 claimed all Swedish names are Wikidata labels or aliases, which is not true for Jörmungand.
findings.resolution: Confirmed live (Q181227 has no Swedish alias Jörmungand; Q1125073 sv label Svadilfare; Q37499380 sv label Ivaldi). Step 4 now names the source of each, step 3 says "except where step 4 says otherwise", and the Swedish Wikipedia articles Midgårdsormen (jormungandr, ragnarok-thor) and Svadilfare (sleipnir-mother, with a Wikidata check on Q1125073's Swedish label) were added as evidence.

findings.issue: Method step 1 said Anderson's Gylfaginning paragraphs run §1–§57.
findings.resolution: Confirmed in pg18947.txt (§58 and §59 follow §57); now §1–§59.

findings.issue: The Swedish note repeated NE's hedge "ungefär", making a verification source the visible model for the wording.
findings.resolution: Now "Namnen betyder ”tanken” och ”minnet”; …", matching the English note and Bellows.

findings.issue: The licensing text did not say on what basis the NE and Swedish Wikipedia quotations in the report are republished, so a reader could take them to be CC0.
findings.resolution: Appended that the CC0 dedication covers the cards only and that these quotations are used under the right of quotation (upphovsrättslagen 22 §) and, for Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0, and are not CC0.

findings.issue: The "Who did the work" paragraph did not name the deck's own machine check, the word-for-word quotation check.
findings.resolution: The marker now reads "a script that matched every quotation word for word against the saved source texts, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators". The quotations added in this review were checked the same way by review1.py (query 11).

findings.issue: The method strings carry their own numbers, so the rendered report shows double numbers and "step 5" points to the wrong list item.
findings.resolution: Not changed here: the numbered prefixes follow the convention of the other authored decks (us-presidents among them), and the rendering is the builder's, which this deck must not change; the step numbers in the text refer to these prefixes consistently.

findings.issue: Queries 5 and 9 were recorded only as helper-script calls, without their URL templates.
findings.resolution: Added the literal templates: wbgetentities with ids=<up to 50 ids>&props=labels&languages=en|sv for claims.py, and https://runeberg.org/eddan/se-NN.html (NN = 01 … 37) for brate.py.

rounds.lens: Re-check of changed cards and a sample (facts, language, documentation)
rounds.scope: The 14 cards changed in rounds 1–3 and every third card (27 distinct cards) against re-downloaded Gutenberg texts, live NE and Swedish Wikipedia pages and live Wikidata (all 124 checks); metadata, the quality-control log and a validation run.
rounds.summary: No errors or warnings; three suggestions, all applied. The gungnir evidence now cites Bellows for the English form Ivaldi, the njord-domain note says the Prose Edda also has him check the fury of fire, and the licensing text says which single Swedish name forms came from the Swedish Wikipedia.

findings.issue: The English backNote's "Ivaldi" was not the form of any source in the card's evidence (Anderson writes Ivald’s / Ivalde, NE Ivaldes).
findings.resolution: Verified in pg73533.txt (downloaded today): Grimnismol 43 reads "did Ivaldi’s sons", and Bellows's note to it says Ivaldi is "known only as the father of the craftsmen-dwarfs who made … also Othin’s spear Gungnir". Both added to the Bellows evidence; method step 4 names Bellows as the source of the English form.

findings.issue: The Prose Edda sentence also has Njord check the fury of fire, which the shortened answer leaves out without saying so on the card.
findings.resolution: Verified in pg18947.txt §23. The answer stays "the wind and the sea" (the domains NE and Bellows also give); the backNote now adds en "The Prose Edda adds that he checks the fury of fire." / sv "Snorres Edda tillägger att han dämpar eldens raseri.", and method step 6 mentions it.

findings.issue: The licensing text said nothing was taken from the Swedish Wikipedia, while method step 4 takes the Swedish name forms Jord and Jörmungand from it.
findings.resolution: The licensing text now says that two single Swedish name forms (Jord, also in Anderson's translation, and Jörmungand) were supplied or confirmed by the Swedish Wikipedia and are facts, not protected wording.

rounds.scope: All 44 cards against the dossier's evidence, with every Anderson and Bellows quotation matched word for word against re-downloaded Gutenberg texts; Swedish names, style and language tags; selection counts, description, keywords and study direction; the fixes of round 4.
rounds.summary: Round 4's fixes were confirmed in place. One warning (thor-mother: the sources give other names for Jord) and two wording suggestions (tyr-hand, gleipnir); all three were verified and applied.

findings.issue: The front has more than one right answer: Anderson's own vocabulary calls Thor's mother Hlodyn and Thor the son of Fjorgyn, so a learner who answers either would be marked wrong.
findings.resolution: Verified in pg18947.txt (Vocabulary "HLODYN. Thor’s mother.", "THOR. Son of Odin and Fjorgyn.", §56 verse "Son of Hlodyn"), pg73533.txt (Voluspo notes 55–56) and Brate's Völuspå 56 ("Lodyns", "Fjorgyns son"). The answer stays Jord, the Prose Edda's main name; the backNote now reads en "Her name means “earth”; she is also called Fjorgyn and Hlodyn. Thor's father is Odin." / sv "Namnet betyder ”jord”; hon kallas även Fjorgyn och Lodyn. Tors far är Oden." The Swedish Lodyn is Brate's form rather than the Swedish Wikipedia's Lödyn that the reviewer suggested, since Brate is a public-domain source already used for Swedish name forms. The quotations were added to the Anderson and Bellows evidence, a Brate entry was added, and method step 4, the licensing text and query 12 record it.

findings.issue: In the backNote, "bound him" / "band honom" can be read as the gods binding Tyr.
findings.resolution: Agreed (Anderson §25: the asas bound the Fenris-wolf). Now en "…while the gods bound the wolf." / sv "…medan gudarna band ulven."

findings.issue: The backNote's "the sound of a cat's footfall" is not the cited translation's wording, "the footfall of cats".
findings.resolution: Verified in pg18947.txt §35. Applied so the note matches the cited source: en "the footfall of cats" / sv "kattens steg".

front.en: Which god is the highest and oldest of the Æsir, called Allfather?
front.sv: Vilken gud är den högste och äldste av asarna och kallas Allfader?

evidence.says: §20: "Odin is the highest and oldest of the asas. He rules all things"; "Odin is called Alfather, for he is the father of all the gods". §3 names the highest and oldest god "Alfather".
"Of all the gods | is Othin the greatest".
"Oden (fornisländska Oðinn), Odin, gud i fornnordisk religion, den främste bland asarna".
Q43610 (Odin): en label "Odin", sv label "Oden", sv alias "Allfader".

front.en: What is Thor the god of?
front.sv: Vad är Tor gud för?

backNote.en: The Prose Edda calls him the strongest of all gods and men.
backNote.sv: Snorres Edda kallar honom den starkaste av alla gudar och människor.

evidence.says: "Thor: the thunder-god, son of Othin and Jorth (Earth)".
§21: "He is the strongest of all gods and men". Anderson's vocabulary: "THOR. Son of Odin and Fjorgyn. The god of thunder."
"är en fornnordisk och forngermansk åskgud"; "starkast av alla gudar och människor".
Q42952 (Thor): en label "Thor", sv label "Tor", P31 (instance of) Q842697 (thunder deity).

front.en: Which god is so fair and bright that light shines from him, the best of the Æsir?
front.sv: Vilken gud är så fager och strålande att det lyser om honom, den bäste av asarna?

evidence.says: "Odin’s second son is Balder, and of him good things are to be told. He is the best, and all praise him. He is so fair of face and so bright that rays of light issue from him".
"Baldr (cf. Voluspo, 32, note), the fairest and best of the gods".
"Balder, fornnordisk gud, son till Oden och Frigg"; "Han är framställd som den ”vitaste” av asagudarna".
Q131658 (Baldur): en alias "Baldr", sv label "Balder".

front.en: What does Njord rule over, according to the Prose Edda?
front.sv: Vad råder Njord över enligt Snorres Edda?

backNote.en: Seafarers and fishermen call on him. The Prose Edda adds that he checks the fury of fire.
backNote.sv: Sjöfarare och fiskare åkallar honom. Snorres Edda tillägger att han dämpar eldens raseri.

evidence.says: "He rules the course of the wind and checks the fury of the sea and of fire. He is invoked by seafarers and by fishermen."
"Noatun (“Ships’-Haven”): the home of Njorth, who calms the waves".
"enligt Snorre Sturlassons Edda härskare över havet och vinden".
Q193879 (Njord): en label "Njord", sv label "Njord".

front.en: What does Freyr rule over, according to the Prose Edda?
front.sv: Vad råder Frej över enligt Snorres Edda?

back.en: rain, sunshine and the fruits of the earth

backNote.en: It is good to call on him for harvests and peace.
backNote.sv: Honom åkallar man för god skörd och fred.

evidence.says: "Frey is the most famous of the asas. He rules over rain and sunshine, and over the fruits of the earth. It is good to call on him for harvests and peace."
"fornnordisk fruktbarhetsgud"; "Enligt Snorre Sturlasson råder han över årsväxt, boskapslycka och fred."
Q131474 (Freyr): en label "Freyr", sv label "Frej", P2925 (domain of saint or deity) Q11663 (weather).

front.en: In what matters is it good to call on Freyja, according to the Prose Edda?
front.sv: I vilka angelägenheter är det enligt Snorres Edda gott att åkalla Freja?

backNote.en: When she rides to battle, half of the slain are hers and half are Odin's.
backNote.sv: När hon rider till strid tillfaller hälften av de stupade henne och hälften Oden.

evidence.says: "Freyja is the most famous of the goddesses"; "when she rides to the battle, one half of the slain belong to her, and the other half to Odin"; "She is fond of love ditties, and it is good to call on her in love affairs."
"Hon har ett vidsträckt maktområde och härskar över liv och död, kärlek och strid, fruktbarhet och svart magi."
Q1647325 (Freyja): en label "Freyja", sv label "Freja", P31 (instance of) Q1670614 (love deity).

front.en: What is Tyr the god of?
front.sv: Vad är Tyr gud för?

backNote.en: He decides victory in war, so warriors call on him.
backNote.sv: Han avgör segern i krig, och därför åkallar krigare honom.

evidence.says: §25: "He is very daring and stout-hearted. He sways victory in war, wherefore warriors should call on him." Vocabulary: "TYR. The one-armed god of war."
"Tyr: the god of battle".
"Tyr framstår som en stark krigsgud."
Q172713 (Tyr): en label "Tyr", sv label "Tyr", P2925 (domain of saint or deity) Q198 (war).

front.en: What is Bragi the god of?
front.sv: Vad är Brage gud för?

backNote.en: The Prose Edda calls him a master skald, famed for his eloquence.
backNote.sv: Snorres Edda kallar honom en mästerskald, berömd för sin vältalighet.

evidence.says: "He is famous for his wisdom, eloquence and flowing speech. He is a master-skald, and from him song-craft is called brag (poetry)".
"Bragi: the god of poetry."
"Brage, i tävlan med Oden skaldekonstens gud i nordisk mytologi."
Q199959 (Bragi): en label "Bragi", sv label "Brage", P2925 (domain of saint or deity) Q482 (poetry).

front.en: What is Heimdall's task among the gods?
front.sv: Vad är Heimdalls uppgift bland gudarna?

backNote.en: He sits at the end of heaven and guards the bridge against the giants.
backNote.sv: Han sitter vid himlens ände och vaktar bron mot jättarna.

evidence.says: "He is the ward of the gods, and sits at the end of heaven, guarding the bridge against the mountain-giants."
"Heimdall: the watchman of the gods".
"Heimdall (fornisländska Heimdallr), gudarnas väktare i fornnordisk religion".
Q131196 (Heimdall): en label "Heimdall", sv label "Heimdall".

front.en: What does the goddess Idun keep?
front.sv: Vad förvarar gudinnan Idun?

back.en: the apples that make the gods young again
back.sv: äpplena som gör gudarna unga igen

backNote.en: She is Bragi's wife.
backNote.sv: Hon är Brages hustru.

evidence.says: "His wife is Idun. She keeps in a box those apples of which the gods eat when they grow old, and then they become young again".
"According to Snorri, the goddess Ithun had charge of the apples which the gods ate whenever they felt themselves growing old."
"Idun (fornisländska Iðunn), gudinna i fornnordisk religion, maka till skaldeguden Brage. Idun bevarar de äpplen som skänker evig ungdom."
Q204691 (Iðunn): en alias "Idun", sv label "Idun", P26 (spouse) Q199959 (Bragi).

front.en: Which god does the Prose Edda call the originator of deceit and the disgrace of gods and men?
front.sv: Vilken gud kallar Snorres Edda svekets upphovsman och gudars och människors skam?

evidence.says: "He is the originator of deceit, and the disgrace of all gods and men. His name is Loke, or Lopt."
"Loki, the trouble-maker, brought the mistletoe to Baldr’s blind brother, Hoth".
"Loke är kraftfull och listig men ständigt svekfull."
Q133147 (Loki): en label "Loki", sv label "Loke", P2925 (domain of saint or deity) Q170028 (deception).

front.en: Who is Thor's mother?
front.sv: Vem är Tors mor?

backNote.en: Her name means “earth”; she is also called Fjorgyn and Hlodyn. Thor's father is Odin.
backNote.sv: Namnet betyder ”jord”; hon kallas även Fjorgyn och Lodyn. Tors far är Oden.

evidence.locator: Gylfaginning §9, §37 and §56 (verse); Vocabulary, HLODYN and THOR

front.en: What is Thor's hammer called?

front.en: What is Odin's eight-legged horse called?

front.en: What are Odin's two ravens called?
front.sv: Vad heter Odens två korpar?

front.sv: Vad heter Odens spjut?

front.en: What is the fetter that holds the wolf Fenrir called?

front.en: What are the women called whom Odin sends to every battle to choose who will be slain?
front.sv: Vad kallas de kvinnor som Oden sänder till varje strid för att välja vilka som ska falla?

front.en: From which giant's body did Odin and his brothers make the world?

Q180682 (Midgard): en label "Midgard", sv label "Midgård", P31 (instance of) Q115410539 (human world).

Q207923 (Muspelheim): en label "Muspelheim", sv label "Muspelhem".

"Niflheim, the world of darkness and the dead".
"Niʹfelhem (fornisländska Niflheim), i fornnordisk religion isriket i norr, ibland metaforiskt om underjorden."
Q176062 (Niflheim): en label "Niflheim", sv label "Nifelhem".

Q172713 (Tyr): en label "Tyr", sv label "Tyr"; Q182560 (Fenrir): sv label "Fenrisulven".

front.en: Which god, guided by Loki, killed Baldr?
front.sv: Vilken gud dödade Balder på Lokes anstiftan?

front.sv: Vem dödar Oden vid Ragnarök?

front.en: Which son of Odin kills the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarök?

evidence.says: "Thor gets great renown by slaying the Midgard-serpent, but retreats only nine paces when he falls to the earth dead, poisoned by the venom that the serpent blows on him."

evidence.locator: Voluspo 56 and the note to it
evidence.says: Stanza: "Nine paces fares | the son of Fjorgyn, And, slain by the serpent, | fearless he sinks." Note: "The son of Fjorgyn: again Thor, who, after slaying the serpent, is overcome by his venomous breath, and dies."
"Vid Ragnarök ska Tor dräpa Midgårdsormen men själv bli dödligt sårad."
"Midgårdsormen (fornnordiska: Miðgarðsormr, ”världsormen”), Jörmungand (Jǫrmungandr, se Etymologi) med flera är ett gudaväsen ur den nordiska mytologin" (the Swedish note's form Jörmungand).
Q181227 (Jörmungandr): P157 (killed by) Q42952 (Thor), sv label "Midgårdsormen"; Q42952 (Thor): P157 (killed by) Q181227 (Jörmungandr).

front.en: Which god does Heimdall fight at Ragnarök, so that they kill each other?
front.sv: Vilken gud strider Heimdall mot vid Ragnarök, så att de dödar varandra?

evidence.says: "Loke fights with Heimdal, and they kill each other."
"I Ragnarök kämpar Heimdall mot Loke och de två dödar varandra".
Q131196 (Heimdall): en label "Heimdall", sv label "Heimdall"; Q133147 (Loki): en label "Loki", sv label "Loke".
